etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English ful, from Old English full (“full”), from Proto-West Germanic *full, from Proto-Germanic *fullaz (“full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”).

Germanic cognates include West Frisian fol, Low German vull, Dutch vol, German voll, Danish fuld, and Norwegian and Swedish full (the latter three via Old Norse). Proto-Indo-European cognates include English plenty (via Latin, compare plēnus), Welsh llawn, Russian по́лный (pólnyj), Lithuanian pilnas, Persian پر (por), Sanskrit पूर्ण (pūrṇá).

See also fele and Scots fou (whence the English doublet fou (“drunk”)). For the "drunk, intoxicated" sense, compare also Swedish full and other Scandinavian languages.

quote.citation: 1976 March 27, F. Dudley Hart, “History of the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis”, in British Medical Journal, volume 1, number 6012, →DOI, →JSTOR, page 763:
quote.text: Anybody can cure a curable disease if he happens to have the right drug at hand, but the treatment of a condition for which there is no positive cure makes much greater demands on the doctor, who has to be practical pharmacologist, human being, psychiatrist, and father confessor—he has, in fact, to be a proper physician in the fullest sense of the word.

quote.citation: 2013 July-August, Catherine Clabby, “Focus on Everything”, in American Scientist:
quote.text: Not long ago, it was difficult to produce photographs of tiny creatures with every part in focus. […] A photo processing technique called focus stacking has changed that. Developed as a tool to electronically combine the sharpest bits of multiple digital images, focus stacking is a boon to biologists seeking full focus on a micron scale.

definitions.definition: Total, entire.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: 'Twas early June, the new grass was flourishing everywheres, the posies in the yard—peonies and such—in full bloom, the sun was shining, and the water of the bay was blue, with light green streaks where the shoal showed.

definitions.definition: Completely empowered, authorized or qualified (in some role); not limited.
(informal) Having eaten to satisfaction, having a "full" stomach; replete.
(informal, with "of") Replete, abounding with.
(informal, of hands, chiefly in the plural) Carrying as much as possible.
(of physical features) Plump, round.
(of the moon) Having its entire face illuminated.

quote.citation: 1969, Alan S. Feinstein, Folk tales from Siam, page 82:
quote.text: For on those evenings, when the moon is full and bright and clear, mothers and fathers in Siam tell their children to look up at the moon and then ask them what they see there.

definitions.definition: (of garments) Of a size that is ample, wide, or having ample folds or pleats to be comfortable.
Having depth and body; rich.
(obsolete) Having the mind filled with ideas; stocked with knowledge; stored with information.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Studies”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC:
quote.text: Reading maketh a full man.

definitions.definition: Having the attention, thoughts, etc., absorbed in any matter, and the feelings more or less excited by it.

quote.citation: 1693, [John Locke], “§7”, in Some Thoughts Concerning Education, London:  […]  A[wnsham] and J[ohn] Churchill, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Everyone is now full of the miracles done by cold baths on decayed and weak constitutions.

definitions.definition: Filled with emotions.

quote.citation: 1848, James Russell Lowell, The Vision of Sir Launfal:
quote.text: The heart is so full that a drop overfills it.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Impregnated; made pregnant.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “(please specify the book number)”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Ilia, the fair,  […]  full of Mars.

definitions.definition: (poker, postnominal) Said of the three cards of the same rank in a full house.
(chiefly Australia) Drunk, intoxicated.

quote.citation: 1925, United States House Committee on the Judiciary, Subcommittee No. 1, Charges Against William E. Baker, U.S. District Judge:
quote.text: Mr. Coniff: That is the only evidence you gave of his being intoxicated, that his hat was on the side?  […]  Mr. Coniff: That is the only indication you gave the committee when you were asked if the judge was full, that his hat was on the side of his head; is that right?

definitions.definition: (archaic) Fully; quite; very; thoroughly; completely; exactly; entirely.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: Prospero:I have done nothing but in care of thee,Of thee, my dear one, thee, my daughter, whoArt ignorant of what thou art; naught knowingOf whence I am, nor that I am more betterThan Prospero, master of a full poor cell,And thy no greater father.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “(please specify the book number)”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  full in the centre of the sacred wood

quote.citation: 1819, John Keats, Otho the Great, act IV, scene I, verse 112:
quote.text: You know full well what makes me look so pale.

quote.citation: 1880, Dante Gabriel Rosetti, William Blake, lines 9–12:
quote.text: This cupboard […]  this other one,  His true wife's charge, full oft to their abode  Yielded for daily bread the martyr's stone,

quote.citation: 1874, James Thomson, The City of Dreadful Night, section IX:
quote.text: It is full strange to him who hears and feels,  When wandering there in some deserted street,  The booming and the jar of ponderous wheels, […]

quote.citation: 1886 October – 1887 January, H[enry] Rider Haggard, She: A History of Adventure, London: Longmans, Green, and Co., published 1887, →OCLC:
quote.text: I turned my head, and as I lay gasping in the throes of that awful struggle I could see that Leo was off the rock now, for the lamplight fell full upon him.

quote.citation: 1910, Emerson Hough, chapter I, in The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Serene, smiling, enigmatic, she faced him with no fear whatever showing in her dark eyes. […] She put back a truant curl from her forehead where it had sought egress to the world, and looked him full in the face now, […].

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English fulle, fylle, fille, from Old English fyllu, fyllo (“fullness, fill, plenty”), from Proto-Germanic *fullį̄, *fulnō (“fullness, filling, overflow”), from Proto-Indo-European *plūno-, *plno- (“full”), from *pelh₁-, *pleh₁- (“to fill; full”). Cognate with German Fülle (“fullness, fill”), Icelandic fylli (“fulness, fill”). More at fill.

definitions.definition: Utmost measure or extent; highest state or degree; the state, position, or moment of fullness; fill.

quote.citation: c. 1606–1607 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Anthonie and Cleopatra”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: The swan's-down feather,  That stands upon the swell at full of tide.

quote.citation: 1693, Decimus Junius Juvenalis, John Dryden, transl., “[The Satires of Decimus Junius Juvenalis.] The Third Satyr”, in The Satires of Decimus Junius Juvenalis. Translated into English Verse.  […]  Together with the Satires of Aulus Persius Flaccus. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Sicilian tortures and the brazen bull,  Are emblems, rather than express the full  Of what he feels.

quote.citation: 1911, Berthold Auerbach, Bayard Taylor, The villa on the Rhine:
quote.text: […]  he had tasted their food, and found it so palatable that he had eaten his full before he knew it.

quote.citation: 2008, Jay Cassell, The Gigantic Book Of Hunting Stories:
quote.text: Early next morning we were over at the elk carcass, and, as we expected, found that the bear had eaten his full at it during the night.

quote.citation: 2010, C. E. Morgan, All the Living: A Novel:
quote.text: When he had eaten his full, they set to work again.

definitions.definition: (of the moon) The phase of the moon when its entire face is illuminated, full moon.

quote.citation: a. 1622, Francis Bacon, Natural History, in The works of Francis Bacon, 1765, page 322
quote.text: It is like, that the brain of man waxeth moister and fuller upon the full of the moon: [...]

quote.citation: a. 1656, Joseph Hall, Josiah Pratt (editor), Works, Volume VII: Practical Works, Revised edition, 1808 page 219,
quote.text: This earthly moon, the Church, hath her fulls and wanings, and sometimes her eclipses, while the shadow of this sinful mass hides her beauty from the world.

definitions.definition: (freestyle skiing) An aerialist maneuver consisting of a backflip in conjunction and simultaneous with a complete twist.
(of the moon) To become full or wholly illuminated.

quote.citation: 1888 September 20, “The Harvest Moon”, in New York Times, retrieved 10 April 2013:
quote.text: The September moon fulls on the 20th at 24 minutes past midnight, and is called the harvest moon.

quote.citation: 1905, Annie Fellows Johnston, chapter 4, in The Little Colonel's Christmas Vacation:
quote.text: "By the black cave of Atropos, when the moon fulls, keep thy tryst!"

quote.citation: 1918, Kate Douglas Wiggin, chapter 29, in The Story Of Waitstill Baxter:
quote.text: "The moon fulls to-night, don't it?"

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English fullen (“to baptise”), fulwen, from Old English fullian, fulwian (“to baptise”), from full- + *wīhan (later *wēon). Compare Old English fulluht, fulwiht (“baptism”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To baptise.

quote.citation: 1610 October, John Foxe, “An Old Ancient Writing Intituled, The Praier and Complaint of the Ploughman”, in Actes and Monuments of Matters Most Speciall and Memorable, Happening in the Church, with an Vniuersall Historie of the Same. […], 6th edition, volume I, London:  […]  [Humphrey Lownes] for the Company of Stationers, →OCLC, book V, page 373, column 2:
quote.text: And thy diſciples fulleden men in thy name, in forgiueneſſe of her ſinnes.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English fullen (“to full”), from Middle French fouler, from Old French foler, fouler (“to tread, to stamp, to full”), from Medieval Latin fullare, from Latin fullo (“a fuller”).

definitions.definition: To make cloth denser and firmer by soaking, beating and pressing; to waulk or walk.
